en: The Sādhana of the King of the Three Samayas (Trisamayarājasādhana).
Toh. no. 3144. Dergé Tanjur, vol. PHU, folios 163r.1–169v.2.
Translated by Abhayākara and Tshul khrims rgyal mtshan.
[Siddham] Homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
In the language of India:
*Trisamayārājasya Sādhana*. In the language of Tibet: *Dam tshig gsum gyi rgyal po’i sgrub pa’i thabs* (The Sadhana of the King of the Three Samayas). Homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas!
I pay homage to the glorious Trisamaya, the source of all prosperity and happiness.
It is like a wondrous wish-fulfilling gem for those exhausted by the miseries of existence.
To the one whose mind is as marvelous as a jewel to those exhausted by the miserable migrations of existence,
the glorious Three Samayas, the source of all excellence and happiness— homage! There indeed exists a correct means for achievement (*sādhana*) taught here by the former masters.
However, for those who fear prolixity, it is taught in brief.
The former masters have stated: "Although there exists an authentic *sādhana*, for those who fear prolixity, I shall provide a concise exposition.

In this regard, indeed, in the *Śrī-Trailokyavaśaṃkara-mahātantrarāja*, a great tantra, a mantra-practitioner who has obtained authorization through the ritual in either a mantra-maṇḍala or a powder-maṇḍala, and who abides by the commitments (*samaya*) and vows (*saṃvara*) prescribed therein, desiring to perform the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*), should dwell in secluded and solitary places that are pleasing to the mind—such as mountains, forests, caves, houses, groves, or mountain retreats.

First, having prepared a mandala strewn with flowers before an image of the Buddha, one should prostrate, generate the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), and dedicate oneself to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. Then, practicing the recitation while focused on that prostration, one should recite this root mantra one thousand times. Thereby, the hundred-thousand-fold recitation for all mantras is accomplished; furthermore, all protective and other such mantras become effective for him.

Having first ensured that one has received empowerment according to the ritual in either a mantra mandala or a colored-powder mandala of this very Great Tantra of the King of the Three Glorious Samayas, and having established oneself in the commitments (samaya) and vows (saṃvara) taught therein, one should go to a cave in a mountain or forest, or to a pleasant house or dwelling.

When one has become secluded and joyful through the entry of the *grul* (spirit), the practitioner should take up residence there. First of all, in the presence of an image of the Buddha, one should scatter loose flowers upon a maṇḍala, prostrate properly, generate the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*), and [take refuge in] the Buddha.

Having focused on offering oneself to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas and prostrating to them, one should perform the recitation five hundred times through practice; this constitutes having performed one hundred thousand recitations for each of all the mantras. Through this mantra, one will also attain accomplishment in all matters such as protection and so forth.

In this regard, the vidyā-mantra is as follows: Homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas! O you who are stainless and the removers of impurity, infinite, together with your sons, all Victors who are without limit or end—grant me the boon; grant me always the most sublime, foremost, and infinite boon.

Now, this is the *vidyā*: Homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas! May all the Victors—immaculate, who purify stains, together with their infinite sons, immeasurable, and bestowers of the ultimate supreme [attainment]—grant it to me!
Grant me all the infinite, most vast, and supreme accomplishments (*siddhi*)!

In this regard, these are the vajra-words: *arara amama samama mantrānantadharmate khaṇa 2 mahāvīrācale | sama 2 asaha mahābale | kaṇa 2 mahāvarāgrike haha 2 vajra vajranaṅkaye (? dhara 2 hūṃ 2 maṇḍalaṃ samabalāgravikrame kuru 2 turu 2 sarvathā sarvaṃ hi jvala 2 agre agriṇi hūṃ phaṭ svāhā ||*
*Samaya asahya*.
For him, these are the vajra words: *ā rara ā samasa samantānantadharmate khana khana mahāvirātsale | sama sama ā sahama hāvale*.

*Ka na ka na ma h’a ba ra gri ke ha ha ha ha badzra badzra dha ye dha ra dha ra hūṃ hūṃ maṇḍala sama bāla āgra vigrame kuru kuru turu turu sarvathā sarvaṃ jvala jvala āgre agriṇi hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā.*

Then, for the sake of exhausting all karmic obscurations, one should recite the hundred-syllable heart-mantra of all the Tathāgatas eight thousand times according to that very same procedure. Karmic obscurations such as those resulting from defiling the True Dharma or the immediate (ānantarya) offenses will be abandoned. And it is this: *Namaḥ traiyadhvikānāṃ tathāgatānāṃ sarvatrāpratihatāvāptidharmatābalinām*.

Oṃ! O you who are unequaled yet equal, whose teaching attains infinity in every direction, remove [all obstacles] twice! Remember, remember the state of the Buddhas' Dharma which is free from passion! Enter twice! You who possess equal power, laugh twice! Triple [your power]! O you whose great and excellent characteristics are like space, blaze! Blaze in the ocean! Svāhā!

Then, for the purpose of exhausting all karmic obscurations, one should recite the hundred-syllable mantra, the essence of all Tathāgatas, eight thousand times according to that very method; thereby, the karmic obscurations such as abandoning the sublime Dharma and the five crimes of immediate retribution will be thoroughly exhausted. These [mantras] are as follows:
Homage to all the Tathāgatas who have gone to the three times, who have attained power through the nature of phenomena that is never impaired.
Oṃ āsa samasa samantato ānantyāvatiśāsani harahara smarasmaranavigatarāgabuddhadharmate sarasara māśāvalāhasahasa satraya satraya gagana mahābala rakṣaṇe jvalajvala nāśagare svāhā.

Thereupon, one should perform the ritual of preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) as a very limb for accomplishing the prosperity of oneself and others. In that regard, having first risen at dawn, one should pay homage with a resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*) to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, one's masters, in this manner:

Then, one should perform the preliminary ritual as a limb for the certain and perfect accomplishment of both oneself and others. In that regard, first rising early in the morning, one should prostrate in this manner with the thought that all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are one's lords:
"In as many world-systems as there are, to all the Victors together with their Sons, I prostrate with body, mind, and speech."
In infinite world systems, to all those Victors together with their Sons, as long as they remain,
I prostrate with my body, speech, and mind.
Then, one should generate the mind of awakening (bodhicitta).
Following that, one should generate the mind of awakening:
"I generate the mind for perfect awakening for the sake of the enlightenment of all embodied beings;
I shall practice the conduct of excellence that brings about the welfare of all sentient beings."
In order to bestow enlightenment upon all sentient beings today, I shall generate the mind of perfect awakening and practice the conduct of excellence that brings benefit to all beings.

Then, for the purpose of destroying all obstacles, one should bind the Vajra-mudrā of Amoghacaṇḍa, the heart-mantra of Acala, and recite it three times. In this regard, this is the Vajra-mudrā: having extended the right hand upward, one should press the tip of the index finger with the thumb; the remaining fingers are marked with the vajra-signature. The mantra is: *namaḥ samantavajrāṇāṃ trāṭ amoghacaṇḍamahāroṣaṇa sphāṭaya hūṃ tramaya 2 hūṃ traṭ hāṃ māṃ*. One should also bind the Svastika-mudrā.

Having formed a fist with the fingers joined together, one should hold the two middle fingers like needles and the two index fingers slightly detached at the tips of the thumbs. The mantra is: Oṃ hara 2 mahānimitta hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.

Then, for the purpose of subduing all obstructors, one should form the mudrā of Vajracaṇḍī and recite the meaningful essence-mantra of Acala three times. In this regard, the vajra-mudrā is as follows: raise the palm of the right hand upward and press the tip of the index finger with the thumb; the remaining fingers possess the characteristics of a vajra.

The mantra is: *Namaḥ sarvavajribhyaḥ, trāta āmogha-candamahāroṣaṇa svāhā hūṃ trāmaya trāmaya hūṃ tatu haṃ mam*. One should also perform the binding of auspiciousness (*svastika-bandha*): interlace the fingers of both hands and draw them inward to form fists.

Extend the two middle fingers straight out; with the tips of the two index fingers, press them slightly without touching the tips of the thumbs, and hold them there. The mantra is: oṃ hara hara mahāni-matte hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.

Then, having performed the cleansing of the mouth and other preliminary rites, seated comfortably upon a pleasant seat, and focusing upon the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas residing in the ten directions before any one of a cloth painting, a manuscript, or a statue, he should prepare a ritual mandala strewn with loose flowers. Having prostrated with all his limbs according to the previous verse and generated the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), he should thus offer himself to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

"I, who am so-and-so by name, offer myself to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas in every way and at all times. May all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas accept me; may the Greatly Compassionate Protectors empower me, and may they become the bestowers of the boon of accomplishment."

Then, having performed the cleansing of the face and other preliminary rites, one should sit upon a comfortable seat. In front of any suitable object such as a thangka, a scripture, or a statue, one should visualize the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas residing in the ten directions and construct a mandala by scattering loose flowers.

As before, having performed a perfect prostration with all limbs using two verses and having generated the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*), one should offer oneself to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas in this way: "I, who am called [name], offer myself to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas."

"I pray that you may always, at all times, properly sustain me. I pray that all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas may grant their blessings upon me. O Protectors endowed with great compassion, this is also my petition for the supreme siddhi."
Then one should confess all misdeeds: "I confess all misdeeds born of passion, hatred, and delusion, belonging to all times, without exception, just as the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, know them."

Then, one should confess all misdeeds: "I shall confess, without exception, all misdeeds arising from desire, hatred, and delusion that occur at all times—just as they are known by the Blessed Buddhas. Thus it is said.

Then, having rejoiced in the merit, one should rejoice with the supreme rejoicing in all the accumulations of merit and wisdom—both mundane and supramundane, belonging to the three times—of all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, just as the Blessed Buddhas know them.

Then, one should rejoice in merit as follows: "I shall perform the supreme rejoicing, just as the Buddha Bhagavāns have rejoiced, in all the accumulations of merit and wisdom belonging to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—whether mundane or supramundane—which are comprised within the three times. Thus it is said.

Then, remaining in the paryanka posture, one should bind this samaya-mudrā: the añjali of salutation placed upon the head is the samaya-mudrā. The mantra is: *namaḥ susiddhe sādhani agre karuṇe varade tayi 2 atibale namo 'stu varasiddhidāyakebhyo mahākṛpebhyaḥ svāhā*. By this, the samaya of all mudrās and mantras is revealed.

Then, remaining well-settled in the cross-legged posture, one should bind this samaya-mudrā: placing the palms joined above the crown of the head is the samaya-mudrā. The mantra for the accomplishment of perfect attainment is: *namastu sarvasiddhida yakṣebhyaḥ*, [the one] who bestows supreme compassion that reaches the ultimate goal, *tatvitatvātibalina*.

*Mahākṛpibhyaḥ svāhā!* These constitute the well-expounded commitments (*samaya*) of all mudrās and secret mantras (*guhyamantra*). Then, having bound the vajra-mudrā as before, one should recollect the heart-mantra of Acala: *Namaḥ samantavajrāṇām, acala kāṇa caṇḍa sādhaya hūṃ phaṭ!*
Then, having bound the vajra-mudrā as before, one should recollect the essence-mantra (hṛdaya) of Acala: *namaḥ samantavajrāṇām ātma-kāyana-canda-sādhaya hūṃ phaṭ*.

Then, one should place the Vajroṣṇīṣa mudrā upon the head. One should form the right fist with the thumb standing upright. The mantra is: *Namaḥ sarvabuddhabodhisattvānāṃ triśikhāgre namo ’stu te | samantād asamantāgre guṇācalāgradharme vidhvanāhi kleśaduḥkhajālaṃ jagataḥ sarvasukhān dadāhi cāśu tatre daṃ trisamaye kuru svāhā* ||
By this, the practitioner does not fall away from the Mahāyāna, and his accomplishment becomes free from obstacles.
...is lost.

Immediately following that, one should place the Vajroṣṇīṣa mudrā upon the head; this involves forming a fist with the right hand and extending the thumb. The mantra is: *namo buddhāya bodhisattvebhyaś ca sarvebhyaḥ | triśikhāya namastu te | samantadeva samantāgṛdhracalāgradharāya me | vidhunā kleśaduḥkham*.
*Khā dzalāna jagataḥ sarva-sukhanādhi-cchuta-tre-dama-tri-samaye kuru svāhā!* By this, the mantrin shall not fall away from the Mahāyāna and shall achieve accomplishment without obstacles.

Furthermore, one should apply the *asahā* great protection (*mahārakṣā*) in five places; it becomes a great protection. Having formed the *añjali* with palms facing upward, place the little fingers and ring fingers in the middle of the hands, with the little fingers pointing outward like needles and the ring fingers slightly bent. One should place the thumbs over them. The middle fingers are like needles, and having bent the index fingers at their sides, one should place them on the third joint. This is the great mudrā named *asahā*. The mantra is: [mantra].
Homage to all Vajras! Oṃ haṃ hūṃ sphāṭayāsaha hūṃ phaṭ!
Furthermore, the peerless great protection (*asamā*) should be arranged in five positions;

it will become a great protection. Forming a *śṛṅkhala* (hook) gesture with the ring fingers and little fingers inserted within, extend the two little fingers outward and touch their tips together. Then, place the two thumbs slightly above the two bent ring fingers without touching them.

Joining the two middle fingers and extending them, with the three joints on their sides slightly bent at the index fingers—this arrangement is the mudrā called "Incomparable. The mantra is: *namaḥ samantavajrāṇām oṃ haṃ hūṃ phaṭ | yāsahe hūṃ phaṭ*.

Then, one should perform the armor-rite with the Mahākavaca-mudrā and the Ajitavajrā [mudrā]: the little finger and thumb are in the shape of a chain (śaṅkalā), while the other fingers have their roots, middles, and tips joined together. This is the Ajitavajrā. The mantra is: *Namaḥ samantavajrāṇām oṃ haṃ hūṃ vajramaye varakavace ho vajra 2 hūṃ phaṭ*.

Then follows the great armor mudrā: one should don the armor of Vajrāparājita. By joining the two little fingers and the two thumbs in the form of a linked chain (*lu gu rgyud*), and properly aligning their bases, middles, and tips with the others, this is Vajrāparājita. The mantra is: *namaḥ samantavajranāma oṃ haṃ hūṃ vajravayavakavace ho vajra vajra hūṃ phaṭ*.
In this way, one becomes utterly invincible to Māra and the other [obstacles].
In this way, one will not be overcome even by Māra and the like.
Having thus performed the protection of oneself, one should perform the protection of the place.
Having thus performed the protection of oneself, one should protect the dwelling place.

Therein, with the *vajrāsana-mudrā*, one should consecrate the seat as being composed of vajra. Having assumed the cross-legged posture (*paryaṅka*), one should place the right hand upon the upturned left hand in the lap; this is the *vajrāsana-mudrā*. The mantra is: *Namaḥ samantavajrāṇāṃ oṃ haṃ hūṃ vajrāsane vaṃ hūṃ phaṭ*.

Thus, one should consecrate the seat as being of the nature of a vajra by means of the Vajrāsana mudrā. Having assumed the cross-legged posture, place the right palm well upon the upturned left palm with its fingers pointing upward; this is the Vajrāsana mudrā. The mantra is: *namaḥ samantavajrāṇām oṃ haṃ hūṃ vajranepaṃ hūṃ phaṭ*.

Then, with the Vajramaṇḍapa-mudrā, one should consecrate one’s own place as consisting of vajra. For the Vajramaṇḍapa-mudrā: with the hands in the gesture of salutation (*praṇāmāñjali*), insert the two index fingers and the two ring fingers—bent at the middle joints—from the inside so that they form the shape of four pillars, while the remaining fingers are in the shape of needles. The mantra is: *namaḥ samantavajrāṇāṃ oṃ haṃ hūṃ vajrāgrabhuvane maṃ hūṃ phaṭ*.

% The Two Threatening Fingers (tarjanīdvaya) % Then, with the mudrā of the vajra-maṇḍala, one should consecrate one’s own abode as being of the nature of vajra: joining the palms together, one bends the middle joints of the two index fingers and the two ring fingers inward and inserts them well, in the manner of pillars.
The manner of forming the remaining [mudrās] of the regions is the vajra-maṇḍala mudrā. The mantra is: *namaḥ samantavajrāṇām oṃ haṃ hūṃ vajrāgrabhuvane loṃ oṃ hūṃ phaṭ*.

Then one should assign the vajra-fence (*vajraprākāra*) with its mudrā. Having formed the *añjali* with palms facing upward, place the two ring fingers (*anāmikā*) in the middle; then, with the two middle fingers acting as needles and the pair of index fingers (*tarjanī*) in the form of a vajra, place them upon the third joint. The two thumbs are on the sides. This is the fence-mudrā. The mantra is: *namaḥ samantavajrāṇāṃ oṃ haṃ hūṃ vajramaṇḍale bandha bandha hūṃ phaṭ*.

Now, since this is the Vajra Fence (*vajraprākāra*), its mudrā should be displayed: with the two ring fingers drawn inside the hollowed palms, the two middle fingers are raised with their tips joined at the third joint; on the side where the two index fingers are arranged in the form of a vajra, the two thumbs are joined together—this is the mudrā of the fence. The mantra is:
*namaḥ samantavajrāṇām oṃ haṃ hūṃ vajramaṇḍale bandha bandha hūṃ phaṭ*.

Then, one should place a vajra-pañjara (vajra-lattice) above that with its corresponding mudrā. For the praṇāmāñjali (salutation-gesture): the pair of ring fingers and the pair of index fingers are bent back against each other at the backs; the middle fingers are like needles, as are the little fingers and the thumbs. This is the pañjara-mudrā. The mantra is: *namaḥ samantavajrāṇāṃ oṃ haṃ hūṃ vajrāgrabhuvane muḥ hūṃ phaṭ*.

*Commentary:* Regarding the phrase "with the backs turned and broken," one should place those same two fingers (the ring and index) upon the wheel with their backs joined and drawn inward. Then, joining the palms together, one should join the backs of the two ring fingers and the two index fingers and draw them inward; the middle fingers are joined at their tips and raised, and the little fingers and thumbs are likewise positioned—this is the mudrā of the pavilion (*guḍa*). The mantra is: *namaḥ*.
The mantra is: *namaḥ samantavajrāṇām oṃ haṃ hūṃ vajragrabhane maḥ hūṃ phaṭ*.

Then, one should project the vajra-flame outside with that mudrā. With the right hand, one should rotate the left hand, which is positioned above [the right] with its fingers clenched. This is the Vajra-flame. The mantra is: *namaḥ samantavajrāṇām oṃ haṃ hūṃ vajrajvāle hūṃ phaṭ*.

Then, externally, there is the blazing vajra; its mudrā is to be formed as follows: having formed the mudrā of fearlessness, one covers it with the fingers of the left hand behind it, while circling with the right hand is the blazing vajra. The mantra is: *namaḥ samantavajrāṇām oṃ haṃ hūṃ phaṭ*.

Then one should bind the boundary. Having raised the index finger with the right fist, one should rotate it to the right. This is called the "boundary-binding" (*sīmābandhanī*). Its mantra is: *namaḥ samantavajrāṇāṃ oṃ haṃ hūṃ mahāsīmābandhe bandha bandha vajre vajriṇi hūṃ phaṭ*.

Regarding the binding of the great boundary (*mahāsīmābandha*): Next, the boundary should be demarcated. One should circle to the right with the right hand in a fist, with the index finger extended. This is the demarcation known as "the absence of intermediate boundaries" (*anantaramadhya*). Its mantra is: *namaḥ samantavajranām ā oṃ haṃ hūṃ maṣī māhāsi mā bandhe bandha bandha vajre vajriṇi hūṃ phaṭ*.

Then, having thus performed the protective enclosure (*rakṣāparikara*), one should offer the guest-water (*argha*) to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas remaining in their own abodes by means of the Tathāgata-sambhava-mudrā. Thereupon, they will take heed of one and become bestowers of the boon of accomplishment (*siddhi*). The Tathāgata-sambhava-mudrā consists of the two little fingers (*kaniṣṭhikā*) extended while the hands are held in the form of a fist. The mantra is: *namaḥ samantabuddhabodhisattvānām āḥ amalavikrāntatejini araje svāhā*.

Having thus performed the protection along with its auxiliary rites, one should then properly announce the news of the appearance of the Tathāgatas and the offering of gifts to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas while remaining in one's own abode. By this, they will hold one in their universal compassion and will also bestow the supreme siddhis.

The mudrā of the appearance of the Tathāgatas is formed by joining the two fists and extending the two little fingers outward. The mantra is: *namo buddhāya bodhisattvāya sarvebhyaḥ | āḥ amala-vikrāntatejini ārajehi svāhā*.

Then, when external offerings such as incense and so forth are available, one should purify them with the Acalavajra-mudrā; having consecrated the incense and other substances eight times each with their respective mantras, one should perform the worship. Therein, the mantra for incense is: *Namaḥ traiyadhvikānāṃ sarvatathāgatānām, asamagandhottame bhagavati, sphārahi maṃ gaganakaṃ mahodaye sarvārthasādhani svāhā*. The mantra for flowers is: [as follows].

Homage to all the Tathāgatas of the three times! O you who possess the great flower that turns and does not turn! Svāhā! This is the incense mantra. Homage to all the Tathāgatas of the three times! O foremost one, O you with the foremost crest, O you with the crest of smoke! Svāhā! This is the lamp mantra. Homage to all the Tathāgatas of the three times! O blazing one, O flaming one, O crest of the light of the lamp! Svāhā! This is the food offering mantra.
Homage to all the Tathāgatas of the three times! Arara parara karara balide, offer the offering, O Great Offering, svāhā!

Then, having purified the external articles of enjoyment, such as perfumes and so forth, with the immovable vajra-mudrā, one should consecrate each of the perfumes and other items eight times with their respective mantras and offer them. In that regard, the mantra for perfume is: "Homage to all the Tathāgatas who have gone to the three times."

"By this incomparable, sublime fragrance of mine, which extensively pervades the expanse of space, may all the purposes of the Blessed One be accomplished: *svāhā*. The mantra for flowers: "Homage to all those who have gone in the three times! Possessing great flowers encircled by a surrounding garland: *svāhā*. The mantra for incense:

Homage to all the Tathāgatas who have gone throughout the three times! Svāhā! At the peak of the peak of the finest incense! Svāhā! The mantra of the lamp is: Homage to all the Tathāgatas who have gone throughout the three times! Svāhā! At the peak of the light of the blazing, flickering lamp! Svāhā! The mantra of the divine food (naivedya) is:
Homage to all the Tathāgatas who have gone throughout the three times! Āra ra para ra kara ra! Having offered the bali, may this great bali-offering presented by me be svāhā!

Then, one should offer the various articles of worship situated in the world-systems of the ten directions as follows: having formed the añjali-gesture of prostration, one should utter these words: "Whatever special articles of worship exist in the world-systems of the ten directions—those that are without 'mine-ness' and without possession; those born on land, such as jewel-mountains, *kalpavṛkṣa* trees, and so forth; those born in water, such as oceanic jewels and so forth; those such as golden lotuses; and whatever other divine or human things there may be in all world-systems, including all forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and textures—all these I offer to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas."
% The Limbs of the Variegated Worship % Then, the other various limbs of worship residing in the world-systems of the ten directions should be offered as follows:

Appending the final syllable of homage (*namo*), one offers those things that have not been claimed as one's own and are free from grasping—whatever exists in the world-systems of the ten directions as varieties of offerings: those born from the earth, such as jewel-mountains and wish-fulfilling trees; those born from water, such as the jewels of the ocean; and those born from golden mud, and so forth.

"Whatever mental objects there may be—namely, all the forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, and so forth of gods and humans throughout all world systems—I shall offer them all to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas by every possible means. This is the illustration (*udāharaṇa*).

One should thus set forth clouds of mental offerings. Having formed the *pūrṇa-mudrā*, characterized by the hands being slightly contracted at the tips in the gesture of reverent salutation (*praṇāmāñjali*), one should speak as follows: "By the power of the empowerment of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, by the power of my own vow and merit, and by the power of the *vidyā-mantras*, may great clouds of sublime and vast offerings, produced through the conduct of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, spread forth into all the maṇḍalas of the assemblies of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. Having thus reflected, [one recites] this mantra which effects the empowerment of the offerings:
One should recite the Queen of Great Knowledge eight times: *Namaḥ sarvabuddhabodhisattvānāṃ sarvathā udgate spharahi maṃ gaganakaṃ samantataḥ svāhā*.

The clouds of offerings consisting of the nature of mind should also be presented in this way: having formed the mudrā of salutation by slightly curling the tips of the fingers and joining the palms together, one should speak as follows:

By the power of the blessings of all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, by the power of my own aspirational prayers and merit, and by the power of the secret mantras of vidyā, [may it be established] within the mandala of the assemblies of all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

One should also reflect: "May a great cloud of offerings, as proclaimed in the *Supremely Vast Conduct of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra*, arise everywhere. Then, one should recite this vidyā-king that empowers the offerings eight times: *Namo buddhānāṃ ca bodhisattvānāṃ sarveṣām | oṃ udgate sphara hi mama kāmagana khaṃ samantataḥ svāhā |*

Then, having reflected: "May oceans of clouds of songs praising the diverse qualities of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and oceans of clouds of Dharma-recitations that purify all world-systems, proceed everywhere," one should recite eight times this Queen of Vidyās who brings forth these clouds of songs of praise: *Namaḥ sarvabuddhabodhisattvānāṃ sarvatra saṃkusumitābhijñārāśini namo ’stu te svāhā.*

Then, one should think: "May all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who purify all world-systems be completely satisfied everywhere by oceans of clouds of melodic sounds endowed with various qualities, and by oceans of clouds of the melodic sound of the Dharma. Thus, one should offer [the clouds] that create a garland of clouds.

This King of Vidyās, which causes clouds of praises and melodic sounds to manifest, should be recited eight times: Homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas! *Sarvatrasaṃkurumitābhijñārāśaye namastute svāhā!*

Then, having reflected: "May clouds of emanations of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, equal in body to all sentient beings everywhere throughout the oceans of all world-systems, emerge from every focal point and pacify all the sufferings of all sentient beings; may they lead them to the attainment of all mundane and supramundane prosperity, up to the purity of the body and so forth of Samantabhadra," one should recite this King of Great Mantras eight times.
Homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas! Homage be to you, O Great Vajra, who brings benefit to all sentient beings! Abide everywhere, having empowered all phenomena! Svāhā!

Then, having emanated from all the clouds of emanations of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas throughout all worlds as many as there are atoms in the ocean of world-systems, may he completely pacify all the sufferings of all sentient beings.

One should also reflect, "Please grant that all mundane and supramundane excellences, from the ultimate purity of the body of Samantabhadra and so forth, may be perfectly attained," and then recite this King of Knowledge (*vidyārāja*) up to eight times: Homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas!
Homage and praise to the Great Vajrasattva! Please remain for the sake of benefiting sentient beings! Please grant your blessings so that all phenomena may be realized for everyone! *Svāhā*.
All of this, beginning with the offerings, arises unfailingly through the power of the mantras and so forth; thus, it should be accepted with faith.
One should have faith that all those [acts] such as making offerings do not become perverted through the power of mantras and the like.

One should dedicate this root of merit toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment in this way: "Just as the Buddha Bhagavāns authorize this dedication of the root of merit, so do I dedicate it; and by this merit, may I fully awaken to enlightenment through the conduct of Samantabhadra, and may I establish all sentient beings also in the purity of the conduct of Samantabhadra."

Those roots of virtue should also be dedicated toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening in this way: "Just as the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, have known through their subsequent realization, so shall I also dedicate these roots of virtue."

"By this root of virtue as well, may I manifest complete awakening through the conduct of Samantabhadra, and may I establish all sentient beings in the complete purity of the conduct of Samantabhadra. Thus [he should think].

Then, for the sake of obtaining the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, one should bind that mudrā and recollect the previously mentioned hundred-syllable mantra, or else the five-syllable one.

Then, for the sake of bringing about the empowerment of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, one should bind that mudrā and recollect the hundred-syllable mantra explained before; or else, the five-syllable one.

Having joined the two hands with their backs touching and the fingers pointing upward, one should hold the two index fingers and the two little fingers in the shape of a hook (*saṃkāla*), and place the two thumbs evenly and facing upward between the needle-like middle and ring fingers. This is the *Śatākṣara-mudrā*. As for the *Pañcākṣara-mudrā*: having formed the hollowed *añjali* gesture, one should press the tips of the two thumbs with the two index fingers; the remaining fingers remain in the same manner, shaped like needles. The mantra is: [mantra].
Homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas! Āḥ Vīra Hūṃ Khaṃ!
One should recollect [it].

With the two hands joined back-to-back, the tips of the fingers are pointed upward; the two index fingers and the two little fingers are linked like a chain, while the two middle fingers and the two ring fingers are extended, with the two thumbs inserted between them and held facing upward—this is the mudrā of the hundred-syllable mantra. The mudrā of the five syllables is as follows:

Joining the palms together, touch the tips of the two index fingers to the tips of the two thumbs; the remaining [fingers] are in the form of needles, just as before. The mantra is: *Namaḥ sarvabuddhabodhisattvebhyaḥ āvīra hūṃ khaṃ*.

Then, one should bind the *samantāvabhāsoṣṇīṣa* mudrā, which is the compendium of all mudrās, or the *dharmacakra* mudrā: with both hands extended and palms turned upward, having placed nail against nail in the middle of the hands between the ring fingers, the little fingers are concealed by the tips of the thumbs and shaped like needles with their ends joined; likewise, the middle fingers are joined at their tips with the nails meeting, while the index fingers are separated in the middle and shaped like needles—this is the *samantāvabhāsoṣṇīṣa*.

Thus, having moved the two index fingers so that the nail touches the nail in a circular shape, this is the Dharmacakra-mudrā. The mantras for these two, respectively, are: ĀḤ MAṂ HAṂ; OṂ DHUNA PĀTAYA CCHINDA CAKREṆA VAJRIṆI HŪṂ. Having bound either one of these two, one should recite the mantra once and then remain standing or seated while performing the recitation (japa). One will not be overcome by Māra and his hosts, and accomplishment (siddhi) will become manifest to him.

Now, one should perform the binding of the Uṣṇīṣa-mudrā, which is the Samantāloka that perfectly gathers all mudrās, or the Dharma-cakra-mudrā: with both hands held level and extended, the ring fingers and index fingers are interlaced within the palms, and the tips of the thumbs are pressed together.

The little finger is extended with its tip joined to the [tip of the] ring finger; the middle finger is likewise raised so that the tips of the nails are level. This is the Uṣṇīṣavijayā mudrā. That itself...

The index fingers are placed together, with the nails slightly touching the nails, forming the shape of a maṇḍala; this is the mudrā of the Wheel of Dharma (dharmacakra). The mantras for these two, in their respective order, are: ĀḤ MĀM HAM and OṂ DYUN PATA YATSCHANA TATSCHRENA VAJRI NĀ HŪṂ.

Having bound either one of these two, one should recite the mantra once; whether walking or sitting, one should perform the recitation, and one will not be overcome by Māra or others. Furthermore, the siddhis will become manifest to this person.

Then, for the sake of swift accomplishment, one should bind the *dharmodaya-mudrā* and recollect its mantra. Having formed a fist with the left hand, one should extend the index finger, the little finger, and the thumb upward; this is the *dharmodaya-mudrā*. The mantra is: *namaḥ samantabuddhabodhisattvānām āḥ sarvathā sarvatrāṇake svāhā*. Having uttered the mantra once with one’s own mudrā, one should display the *samaya*. One’s own mudrā, however, should be understood according to the appropriate application.
One should recollect [it].

For the purpose of swift accomplishment, one should then form the *dharmodayā* mudrā and recite its mantra. Forming a fist with the left hand, with the index finger, little finger, and thumb extended upward, is the *dharmodayā* mudrā. The mantra is: *Namaḥ sarvabuddhabodhisattvebhyaḥ āḥ*.
*Sara patha sarpatrana ke svāhā*. By reciting this mantra once along with one's own mudrā, the samaya is made firm. One should also understand one's own mudrās as appropriate.

Then, practicing the recitation while taking as one's object of focus the prostration to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, one should recite the desired mantra—neither too fast nor too slow, free from improper thoughts, with the mind fixed upon the syllables of the mantra—for as long as no fatigue arises.

Then, visualizing the prostration with the five limbs to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, one should practice the recitation. Abandoning conceptualizations that are neither too fast nor too slow, one should recite with a mind focused on the mantra-syllables as a vidyā-mantra for as long as one does not become weary.
Then, having risen, one should recite the noble *Gaṇḍavyūha* and other sūtras after having once called to mind the *Tathāgatagarbha*.
Then, having risen, one should recite the noble *Gaṇḍavyūha* and other sūtras after having once called to mind the *Tathāgatagarbha*.

Having made offerings, or at least having prostrated, one should eat. While eating, one should consecrate the food eight times with this mantra and, after offering the first morsel (*agrapiṇḍa*) to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, one should eat in moderate measure. Here is that mantra: *Namaḥ sarvabuddhabodhisattvānāṃ oṃ balandade tejomālini svāhā*. From the remains of the meal, one should offer a discarded morsel (*utsṛṣṭapiṇḍa*) after consecrating it once with the heart-mantra of Noble Acala Amogha-caṇḍa.

Being constantly attended to, it bestows the accomplishment of happiness. And having rested after eating and performed the confession of misdeeds and so forth, one should remain solely devoted to the delight of the True Dharma.

Finally, one should offer worship, prostrate, and then eat the food. While eating, one should consecrate it eight times with this mantra; the first portion should be made into an offering for all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and the remainder should be eaten in moderate measure. In this regard, the mantra is as follows:

Homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas! Oṃ baladānavīryamālā svāhā! Having recited this mantra once over the remains of what has been eaten, one should offer those remaining morsels with the heart-mantra of the noble Acala Caṇḍa Amogha.

Those who follow [the practice] constantly will be granted the attainment of siddhi. Even after eating and resting, one should perform the confession of misdeeds and so forth, and abide in a state of delight in the sublime Dharma.

If one is able, then even in the afternoon, having performed all these preparations for protection and so forth, as well as the worship and so on, one should perform the recitation (*japa*). If not, then having firmly resolved that the protection and other rites performed in the forenoon remain undismissed and established, one should dispel obstacles with the Noble Acala-vajra-mudrā accompanied by its mantra; then, having performed protection with any one of the five-syllable mantras and so forth together with their respective mudrās, and having carried out the worship, praise, and so on, one should perform the recitation as before. [The worship and so forth...]

If one is able, then in the afternoon as well, one should perform all those [rites], such as the protection and so forth along with their branches, as well as the offerings and so forth, and then carry out the recitation. If one is unable, then by means of the protection and so forth performed in the morning itself, without requesting the departure [of the deities], one should remain [in that state] and stabilize one's intention.

Having expelled the obstructors with the mantra and mudrā of the noble Acala-vajra, and having performed protection with any other suitable [mantra] such as the five-syllable [om maṇi padme hūṃ] together with its mudrā, one should also employ offerings, praises, and so forth, and perform the recitation as before.

And at the improper time, having cast aside the enclosure, cage, and so forth, one should form the armor (*kavaca*) with the *Raśmimālinī* [mudrā]. Having made a fist with the fingers interlocked on the inside, one should extend the two middle fingers in the shape of a needle and place the pair of index fingers upon its third joint; the two thumbs are placed on the sides. This is the *Raśmimālinī* mudrā. The mantra is: [Mantra follows]

Homage to the Tathāgatas of the three times! O you who have attained the state of the Great Samaya, O equanimous one, O equal one in every respect, O protector of sentient beings, O you who are utterly unattached to the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), svāhā!

One should request the [deity] to depart by means of the sun, a wall, a tent, and so forth, and then perform the ritual of the garland of light rays (*raśmimālā*). The mudrā of the garland of light rays is as follows: with the fingers interlaced, form fists inwardly and extend the two middle fingers outward like needles; at their third joint, place the tips of the two index fingers against each other, and join the two thumbs to their sides. This is the mudrā of the garland of light rays.

The mantra: Homage to all the Tathāgatas who have gone throughout the three times! O you who have realized the great samaya, who have attained the realization of equality, who protect all sentient beings with an equanimous mind, and who are utterly unattached within the dharmadhātu! Svāhā!

During the first and last watches of the night, one should remain awake through practices such as the recitation of the sublime Dharma (*saddharma-svādhyāya*). During the middle watch, one should lie down on a bed devoid of high couches while prostrating with all one’s limbs to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. One should also make this formal petition (*vijñapti*): "May all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas empower me; may they grant the boon of supreme accomplishment (*anuttara-siddhi*) and may they pacify all calamities."

During both the first and last watches of the night, one should not sleep, but should engage in activities such as reciting the sublime Dharma. During the middle watch as well, one should lie down on a bed that has been cleared of a throne, having prostrated properly with all limbs to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

One should also make this request: "I pray that all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas may grant me their blessings; I pray that you may bestow upon me the supreme, unsurpassed attainments; and I pray that you may thoroughly pacify all harms and obstacles."

This same procedure is to be performed daily until the full moon, or until one hundred thousand recitations are completed, or until the signs of accomplishment (*siddhinimitta*) appear. Then, on the lunar days beginning with the full moon, having observed a fast by abstaining from food, and being bound by the *poṣadha* vows, seated upon young shoots or seated upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass before any one of the following—a shrine, a cloth painting, a manuscript, or an image—one should scatter flowers over a mandala and prepare the necessary equipment for protection and worship. Having formed the *dharmodayā* as before, one should recollect that mantra. [Having observed a fast by abstaining from food.]
Regarding this very ritual procedure: one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times every day until the full moon, or until signs of accomplishment have arisen.

Then, on the lunar date of the full moon or other such dates, having fasted and refrained from eating, and being endowed with the vows of the *upavāsa* (one-day observance), one should remain seated upon a seat of leaves or properly settled upon a cushion of *kuṇa* grass.

In front of any suitable object, such as a stūpa, a thangka, a volume of scripture, or an image, one should prepare a maṇḍala completely filled with flowers. The preliminary branches, such as the protection and offerings, are to be performed as before; having bound the source of phenomena (dharmodaya), one should recollect its mantra.
Then, having formed the mudrā of one’s own deity and recited its mantra seven or eight times, one should display the pledge (samaya).
Then, having bound the mudrā of one's own deity, one should stabilize the samaya by reciting its mantra seven or eight times.

Then, having prostrated to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas and taken up the wheel, vajra, and so forth, while aspiring for the purification of the body and other aspects of the Samantabhadra Tathāgata, and fixing one's heart upon the accomplishment of one's own desired goal, one should practice the recitation focused on the prostration to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. With a mental state cultivated through the rejoicing in the accumulations of merit and wisdom of all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, one should recite from the time of the evening twilight until midnight or sunrise; at that point, that wheel and so forth will certainly [manifest].

It blazes forth. And when it has blazed, there appear from the sky most wonderful signs—such as the appearance of a Buddha, rains of flowers, the sounding of drums, divine voices, and the exclamation of "Well done! by the Tathāgatas—as well as the trembling of the Buddha-fields and other such marvels. Furthermore, all the families of vidyādharas assemble.

Consecrated by them, he becomes a king of the vidyādharas who propitiates all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas throughout all world-systems, possesses the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*), is delighted by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and practices the conduct of a Bodhisattva. Surrounded by an infinite retinue of vidyādharī women, he experiences happiness and does not depart from that body. By means of that very body, through the gradual accumulation of the provisions (*saṃbhāra*), he traverses all the Bodhisattva stages (*bhūmi*) until he attains perfect awakening (*abhisaṃbudhyate*).
Then the Vidyādhararāja,

having prostrated with the five limbs to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and holding a wheel, a vajra, or the like, desiring the purification of Samantabhadra, the bodies of the Tathāgatas, and so forth, should bring to mind the siddhi as being close at hand.

One should recite while focusing on the thorough recognition of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; with a mind that has become habituated to rejoicing in the accumulations of merit and wisdom of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, one should recite from sunrise until midnight or until sunrise.

One should perform [the ritual]. From those [mantras], the wheel and so forth will certainly blaze. From that blazing, there will arise great omens similar to the appearance of a Buddha: a rain of flowers falling from the sky, the sound of drums and conchs, the melodies of divine substances, and the "Excellent! (Sādhu! and other such words spoken by the Tathāgatas.

Marvelous events, such as the shaking of the buddha-fields, will occur. All the families of vidyādharas will also gather together, and they too will confer empowerment. One will please the buddhas and bodhisattvas in all world systems and become endowed with the five superknowledges.

All the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas will be greatly delighted; one will become a Vidyādhara King who practices the conduct of a Bodhisattva, endowed with an infinite retinue of Vidyādharas, and bliss will increase. Furthermore, that very body shall not perish.
Having personally accumulated the necessary provisions through that very body, one correctly traverses all the bodhisattva stages until the attainment of manifest, complete enlightenment.

Furthermore, other mundane and supramundane accomplishments—such as beholding the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, the wish-fulfilling gem, the auspicious jar, and so forth—should be accomplished by those free from doubt through this very procedure, or through the procedure seen in the general and specific chapters, after having consulted the tantra; they will certainly succeed.

Furthermore, all mundane and supramundane accomplishments—including the vision of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, as well as the wish-fulfilling gem, the auspicious vase, and so forth—should be accomplished by means of this very method: either by seeing the general and specific chapters, or by properly examining the tantra according to the ritual procedures and thereby eliminating all doubt.
In this way, they will certainly be accomplished.

Thus is the method of accomplishment for those possessing skillful means (*upāya*). However, by those lacking such means, the practice must be performed according to their capacity. One should not despair, thinking, "I am unable [to perform] what has been taught. At the very least, having established even a single protection for oneself, having performed the binding of the boundary (*sīmābandha*), and having contemplated the worship and so forth, one should recite the mantras of that [deity] and perform the recitation (*japa*) or the accomplishment (*sādhana*) as long as desired. According to one's vigor and according to one's action, success will certainly be attained.

For it is stated in the Tantra: "Even a single [deity] is capable of protecting the three worlds. And this Amoghasiddhi is the King of the Three Samayas; he is the unimpeded accomplishment. Furthermore, in this context, mantras being practiced succeed by whatever method or according to whatever one desires. [Note:

The manuscript gloss explains that "the method of one's desire" means performing the mantra practice with a mind intent on the welfare of the world, having merely taken as an object all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, while being devoid of the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) and so forth.]

This is the ritual procedure for the sādhana endowed with skillful means; since it is also to be accomplished even by one devoid of skillful means, one should not become discouraged by thinking, "I am incapable of performing what has been explained. At the very least, one should perform at least self-protection alone; one should mentally visualize the boundary-enclosure, the offerings, and so forth, and recite their mantras.

One should recite it for as long as one desires. Once it has been accomplished, it will certainly succeed in accordance with diligence and in accordance with one’s karma; for it is stated in the Tantra: "Even a single [recitation] is capable of protecting the three worlds."

This King of the Three Samayas is accomplished with purpose and accomplished without obstacles; furthermore, it is accomplished if one practices it while being skilled in those mantras and whichever specific rituals are required.

As it is said in this very [text]: "In a secluded and solitary place, by one who avoids social distraction, who does not deceive sentient beings, [the goal] must certainly be accomplished—even without worship, even without a painted image (paṭa), even without the practice of bathing and so forth, and even if one has fallen into misfortune.
Even without worship, even without a painted image.

This very point was also stated as follows: In a secluded place free from the bustling of worldly people, those who have completely abandoned social gatherings and possess compassion for sentient beings will—despite engaging in conduct that is devoid of ritual offerings, lacks formal measurements, and is not accompanied by rites such as ritual bathing—nevertheless succeed in accomplishing whatever is to be achieved.

It is further stated: "There are two things that are utterly marvelous: in whatever manner the mantras are practiced, in that very manner they become concordant; and by whichever procedure they are applied, by that very one they are accomplished.

It is also stated again: "There are two things that are utterly marvelous: in whatever manner the mantras are practiced, in that very manner they become concordant; by whichever application they are practiced, by that very one they are accomplished."
For one whose bodhicitta is firm and whose mind is free from attachment, no doubt should ever be entertained; for such a person, this will certainly be accomplished.
Thus [it is said].
Furthermore, it is said:
"Those whose bodhicitta is firm And whose intellect has become free from attachment— They should never harbor doubt; Through that, they will always abide in accomplishment."
Thus it is said.
Therefore, having generated diligence and abandoned doubt, one should practice; it will certainly succeed.
Therefore, one should accomplish [the goal] by generating diligence and abandoning doubt; thus, it will certainly be achieved.

And in this regard, one who seeks accomplishment must be exceedingly diligent in guarding the commitments (*samaya*), for all accomplishments have their root therein. Furthermore, that commitment consists of: the true Dharma must not be rejected; no disrespect toward the gurus should be shown; no drinking of intoxicants should be done; no sleeping on a bedstead should be done; and the *vajra*-shaped [substances] must not be consumed nor stepped over—such things as these must necessarily be known from the Tantra. However, they are not written here for fear of prolixity.

In this regard, those who seek accomplishment must exert themselves greatly in guarding the commitments (*samaya*), for all the accomplishments of fortunate individuals arise from that root. Furthermore, those commitments are as follows: one must not abandon the sublime Dharma; one must not show contempt toward the guru; one must not drink intoxicants; and one must not sleep on a high bed.

Regarding the statements such as "one should neither consume nor swallow [substances] of the Vajra family," these should be understood from the tantras; they have not been written here for fear of excessive prolixity.

And by one who desires to bathe, having recited the mantra three times, the following should be performed with the heart-mantra of Noble Acala, namely Amoghacaṇḍa, joined with the vajra-mudrā: the consecration of all bathing substances such as clay and so forth, the expulsion of malevolent beings, and the binding of the boundary; by that alone, all obstacles are pacified.

Even if one wishes to perform ablutions, one should do so while possessing the very essence of the Noble Acala-Amoghasiddhi Vajracanda as taught in the *Tri-samaya*; thus, one should take up the substances for bathing such as cleansing clay and so forth, and perform the subduing of malevolent spirits, the drawing of boundaries, and so on with mantras.
By these very means, all obstacles and the like will be thoroughly pacified.
The *Sādhana* of the King of the Three Samayas is completed. This work is the composition of the scholar Paṇḍita Kumudākaramati.

The *Sādhana of Trisamayavyūharāja* is complete. It was composed by the great paṇḍita Kumudākaraśrī. It was translated by the monk Tsultrim Gyaltsen of the Patshap lineage, in the presence of the paṇḍita Abhayākaragupta.
